title: In his image (CCC 356–357)
hook: every human being is someone, not something

segments.voice: Yesterday, angels: spiritual messengers, and, the Church says, a guardian beside each person. Your line was never alone. Did you catch a moment when you felt accompanied? Today, the creature those guardians are sent to watch over. Day three hundred one.

Listen to how we talk about people on an ordinary day. The delivery. The new hire. The guy in 4B. My ride is two minutes away. The customer on line three. None of it is cruel. It's just fast. A person becomes the job they're doing for us, and we move on. The first chapter of the Bible says the opposite. It puts an invisible mark on every one of those people: this one was made on purpose, to the image of God. The Catechism turns it into a short phrase: a person is someone, not something.
screen: `THE DELIVERY. THE NEW HIRE. THE GUY IN 4B.`
`A MARK YOU CAN'T SEE.` → `SOMEONE, NOT SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: Start with the text. On the sixth day, in the Douay-Rheims, God says: "Let us make man to our image and likeness." And then: "And God created man to his own image: to the image of God he created him. Male and female he created them." In Latin, image of God is imago Dei, and that's today's word. Second, what an image was. In the ancient world, some scholars point out, kings set up statues of themselves in the lands they ruled, a way of saying: I'm present here, this belongs to me. Genesis takes that royal idea and hands it to everyone. Not only the king. The farmer, the servant, the child. Every human being is God's image set down in the world. Third, what the Catechism does with it. It teaches that the human person is the only creature on earth God willed for its own sake, and that each of us is able to know ourselves, to give ourselves freely, and to enter into friendship with God. That's why the Church says a person has dignity: not a thing to be used, but someone. Early Christian writers added a detail. Some, like Irenaeus, told image and likeness apart. The image, they said, is never lost. The likeness, a life that actually resembles God, can be damaged and restored. Fourth, the hard part. The image is in everyone or it means nothing. The person you admire, yes. And the person who cut you off in traffic, the prisoner, the stranger whose language you don't speak, the baby, the dying. Catholics ground their social teaching right here: in this one verse about who we are.
screen: `TO THE IMAGE OF GOD HE CREATED HIM.` · `A KING'S STATUE, GIVEN TO EVERYONE.` · `WILLED FOR ITS OWN SAKE.` · `IN EVERYONE, OR IT MEANS NOTHING.` · then, large: `SOMEONE, NOT SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at someone as God's image. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one face you saw today, maybe someone you barely noticed: the cashier, a driver, a coworker. Hold their face for a moment. Say to yourself, quietly: someone, not something. Then, if you can, bring to mind a face that's harder, someone who annoys you. Hold that face too. You don't have to feel warm. Just let them be a person for a minute. If you pray, you can offer each face to God. The bell holds the time.
Imago Dei. Latin for the image of God: what Genesis says every human being is made in, and why the Church says each person has a dignity no one can take away. Today's word.

Your line: someone, not something. Today, learn or use the name of one person you usually only see as a job. This week ran from I am who am to charity, the Trinity, creation, evil, angels, and now us. Day three hundred one.

howItsDone: Catholics learn in catechism that every person is made in the image of God, and the Church's social teaching on the poor, the unborn, the sick, migrants and prisoners is built on that dignity.

fork.setup: in the ancient world, a king set up statues of himself to show who ruled a land. how does Genesis use the idea of an image?
options: it gives the image only to the priests.
it gives the image to every human being.
it forbids the idea of an image entirely.
fork.reveal: every human, male and female, is made to the image of God. a royal idea becomes everyone's dignity.

original.note: Hebrew: in the image of God. Latin renders it imago Dei.

trapdoor: what you thought: people look a bit like God.
what it means: every person, without exception, is made on purpose and bears a dignity that isn't earned.
what a scholar hears: tselem, a word used for statues and images; the royal image given to all humanity; Irenaeus's split of image and likeness.

sources.quoted: Let us make man to our image and likeness.
And God created man to his own image: to the image of God he created him. Male and female he created them.

notes: Douay-Rheims Genesis 1:26 and 1:27 given from memory; confirm wording and punctuation.

CCC 356–357 paraphrased ('willed for its own sake' comes via Gaudium et Spes 24; 'someone, not something' paraphrases CCC 357). The Catechism's English translation is under copyright, so no direct quotation.
The royal-statue reading of the image is a common scholarly view, not settled doctrine; framed as 'many scholars point out'.
Irenaeus's image/likeness distinction: reference given as Against Heresies 5.6.1; confirm the passage.
Week-end look-back names days 295–301; confirm the week boundary.
